questions.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(2-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+18{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(3\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{2},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2-(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =2-2{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095010/assets/f74113e44d4087a1aa705779b1908341bd580851e98ecda7cf06499188ad4158.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{x}{2y}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=18,$ located in the first quadrant, shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $\sqrt{2}$ and $3,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{7{cos}^{2}⁡t+2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{7{cos}^{2}⁡t+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{2y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{2y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{7{cos}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{7{cos}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095010/assets/ff5883b08bdd339549d03542b87da900ab014954bc52764d0e5da087a72c1e95.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}xy\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+81}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse $25{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=225,$ located in the third quadrant, shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $5,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+9}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+81},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\sqrt{16(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+81} \\  & =15\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16(9{cos}^{2}⁡t)+81} \\  & =15\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{9(16{cos}^{2}⁡t+9)} \\  & =45\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+81}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}45\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+9}\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+9}\,\text{d}t \\  & =45{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(16{cos}^{2}⁡t+9)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy\sqrt{4+3{y}^{2}}$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{12{sin}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4+12{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4(1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy\sqrt{4+3{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{4+3(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4+12{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4(1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\sqrt{4+3{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot 2\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}32{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{32}{6}{\int }_{1}^{1}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}{|}_{1}^{1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{5xy}{3}$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+5{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4+5{cos}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{5xy}{3}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{5}{3}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t=10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}18xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{4+5{cos}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =10{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4+5{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4+5{cos}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}10{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4+5{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{9}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{9}^{9} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$
